current_episode.title: How Wealthy People Buy Cars (Cash vs. Finance vs. Lease)

guest.bio_context: Ryan is currently in the process of buying a car for the first time in 15 years and approaches this episode as a listener seeking guidance. He drives a 2018 F-150 that he plans to keep until it dies, with the goal of passing it to his oldest son as his first car when he turns 16.

context.real_quote: Cars are where good savers go to quietly leak wealth. Not because a car is evil, but because the way most people buy cars is designed to keep them broke.
key_stats: $24,000 — purchase price paid for one-year-old F-150 with 12,000 miles (2019)
$30,000 — depreciation difference on Chevy Suburban between brand new and two years used with less than 30,000 miles
$150 — cost of independent mechanic inspection at dealership or mobile visit
3.5% to 4% — current high-yield savings account interest rate
15–25% — typical depreciation hit for a brand new car in first year
20% — recommended down payment on financed vehicles to avoid being underwater
4 years — maximum recommended loan term (24-12-10 rule: part four stands for four years or less)

pending_qa.q: How can you verify the condition of a used car before purchasing it with cash?
pending_qa.r: Take the vehicle to a local mechanic you know, like, and trust, or have them come to you for about $150. This $150 insurance policy can reveal critical issues that disqualify the purchase, and mechanics often provide a detailed list that you can then use as a negotiation piece with the dealer. If the dealership won't allow this, you can have the mechanic come to the lot instead.

pending_qa.q: How can you accumulate enough cash to purchase the next car without financing?
pending_qa.r: Once your current car is paid off, take the monthly payment amount you were making and continue depositing it into a high-yield savings account. If your payment was $500 per month and you drive cars for 7 to 10 years, you will accumulate over $50,000 set aside for your next vehicle purchase, allowing you to pay cash.

pending_qa.q: What is the risk of being underwater on a financed vehicle, and how does a 20% down payment protect you?
pending_qa.r: When you finance a vehicle, it depreciates immediately upon leaving the lot by 15%, 20%, or 25% depending on the vehicle type. If you total the car a month later, you could owe more than its worth and be unable to sell it. A 20% down payment ensures you are not underwater on the vehicle and effectively prepays the depreciation in the first year, avoiding the need for gap insurance.

pending_qa.q: Should you invest money instead of paying cash for a car if you can get 0% or 1% financing?
pending_qa.r: Even with 0% or 1% financing, you must factor in the vehicle's depreciation. If you buy a $50,000 car at 0% financing and it depreciates to $30,000 in one year, you still owe close to $50,000 on it. You would be underwater and unable to sell without losing money. You must have cash set aside to cover the difference if you need to get rid of the vehicle, and even high-yield savings accounts currently offer 3.5% to 4%, which beats 1% financing.
